correctness.rationale: For s=t−ρ the bounds put s strictly between H(t−2ρ) and H(t), both in the history/trajectory domain. Thus the continuous strict inverse defines a continuous retarded argument. With H(d)=s, sign(g(d))=sign(s−d), and strict order gives sign(s−d)=sign(H(s)−H(d))=sign(Ψ(g(s))); this works at zero even if the relay takes an independent value there. It gives the reference equation almost everywhere. On each compact forward interval a competitor's continuous positive delay has a positive minimum. Advancing in steps shorter than this minimum forces each competing algebraic root to be evaluated on the already agreed history; injectivity of H identifies the reference root. Equality of right-hand sides almost everywhere and absolute continuity propagate equality of states, then roots, on the whole interval. This needs no order assumption on the competitor. The one-sided slope criterion gives H(v)−H(u)≥(1−q)(v−u). I checked the periodic pieces glue, their slopes are 0, 2 and −1/2, and the forcing can be set to zero at the corners to make it bounded and periodic. For all s in (0.24,0.26), the nested arguments are s, −s, 3s, s−1 and then alternate s+1 and s−1, by the plateaus of g; even samples are negative throughout that interval. The implicit root there is s/3 with positive sample, as is the constant-delay sample. This proves a discrepancy on an interval, not a single exceptional time. The frozen witness checker was read, not executed; the interval calculation verifies the witness analytically.

value.rationale: The condition distinguishes well-posedness and unchanged dynamics of the implicit model from success of the natural nested iteration. It is verifiable on a reference history and admits positive slopes forbidden by contraction, while the explicit periodic example forces an actual wrong relay response on a time interval for each even nesting order. This is a usable extension and a concrete warning about substituting nested equations, not a claim about arbitrary nonmonotone branches or physical sinusoidal forcing.
